topic: Space-Filling Curves: Bridging the Finite and the Infinite
target_audience: University students (STEM majors or interested laypeople)

sections.title: The Intuitive Paradox (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the standard dimension concept: lines are 1D, planes are 2D. Pose the question: Can a continuous 1D line ever fill a 2D square completely? This challenges the intuition that dimension is an absolute barrier.
sections.example: Visualize a thin, elastic string being stretched and folded repeatedly until it touches every single point inside a square frame.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Limit Process (0:45-1:45)
sections.content: Explain the concept of an 'Iterative Procedure'. Introduce the idea that while a finite step is just a line, the 'limit' of an infinite sequence of steps results in a new geometric property. This is the bridge between finite math (steps) and infinite math (the limit object).
sections.example: Using a recursive drawing of the Peano curve: Step 1 shows a simple 'S' shape; Step 2 shows a more complex 'S' fold; Step 3 shows a dense zig-zag. The animation zooms out to show the density increasing toward the limit.

sections.title: The Peano Curve Construction (1:45-3:15)
sections.content: Walk through the logic of Giuseppe Peano's construction. Explain how the curve maps the unit interval [0, 1] onto the unit square [0, 1]x[0, 1] continuously. Emphasize that every coordinate in the square corresponds to a specific parameter on the line.
sections.example: A pixel-based animation where a 'scouting robot' travels along a path that bends strictly according to a 3x3 grid rule, demonstrating that no 'gap' is left behind as the iteration depth increases.

sections.title: Conceptual Synthesis: Finite vs. Infinite (3:15-4:15)
sections.content: Discuss why this matters: the curve is continuous but nowhere differentiable. It demonstrates that the distinction between 1D and 2D depends on how we define space. The infinite process transforms a 'thin' object into a 'dense' one.
sections.example: A visual comparison showing a 'finite' step count on one side vs. an 'infinite' blur that perfectly fills the square on the other, highlighting the transition from discrete segments to a continuous area.

sections.title: Real-World Application & Closing (4:15-5:00)
sections.content: Connect the theory to practical uses like image processing (Hilbert curves for memory optimization) and space-filling antennas. Summarize that infinity is not just 'a lot', but a transformative tool in mathematics.
sections.example: Show a smartphone antenna (fractal design) that packs a long wire into a small space, allowing it to capture multiple radio frequencies—the space-filling curve in action.
